problem_data.story:
The Sanctuary for Ethan

Ethan Reid pressed his body against the cold metalite wall of the immigration processing center in Lakeside, Selvoria, the fugitive following silently in his mind.

His fear-driven gaze swept across the crowded detention hall. The place was a pressure cooker of humanity, filled with people culled from every corner of three continents. Most of the vast room lay obscured behind a shimmer of body heat and the acrid smell of unwashed clothes and desperation.

Here and there, Ethan saw moving figures. He could not tell if they were refugees, economic migrants, or political dissidents like himself.

*You've got to find him*, he thought, scanning the crowd. *It's the only way you can escape the dead man.*

Someone tugged at his worn jacket. He jumped, thinking absurdly that it was the dead man's hand reaching from memory.

"You need help, friend?" a small voice asked in broken English. "I know people. Good people. Can get you papers. Real papers. Yes?"

Ethan looked down.

The speaker was an eager-eyed boy of about twelve, thin as a rail, with dark skin and darker eyes. He wore a stained t-shirt advertising a film production company and torn jeans.

"I'm looking for someone," Ethan muttered before he could stop himself.

"Ah, American! I speak English good, yes? Who you look for? I know many people in Lakeside. I find anyone for you, friend."

Ethan shook his head.

He thought, *I don't want your forged documents. I don't want your black market contacts or your smuggling routes. But if you had something that could erase the memory of what I did, I'd pay everything I have.*

"No deal, friend? Then I show you to safe corner. Free. No charge."

The boy grabbed his hand. Because Ethan could think of no reason to resist, he followed. They wove through shifting masses of people and past the drone of multilingual conversations.

They passed the processing desks with their line of stern-faced immigration officers—bureaucrats with the power to grant hope or deliver despair with a single stamp.

They squeezed down a narrow corridor flanked by holding cells that jutted up into the fluorescent brightness like concrete tombstones.

Several times, Ethan glimpsed the bulky figures of Dravonian security guards, the first he'd encountered since crossing the border.

They were massive men, gray-uniformed, silent giants with neural scanners clipped to their belts. They stood solitary and motionless, aloof, their cold eyes unblinking. According to rumors, some of them had been trained in advanced interrogation techniques involving psychological profiling, and the thought sent a fresh rivulet of fear down Ethan's spine.

Once he spotted a blue-uniformed officer of Lakeside's Border Patrol. The woman was striding down a corridor, idly tapping her stun baton against the concrete walls.

*Keep walking*, Ethan told himself. *You look the same as anyone else here. Keep walking. Look straight ahead.*

The officer passed. Ethan breathed easier.

"Here we are, friend," the boy said. "A good spot. Hidden from cameras."

Ethan winced. How did this kid know he wanted to avoid surveillance? Frowning, he sat down on a metal bench—he and the ghost of the dead man.

He listened to the mournful sounds of a street musician's violin drifting through an air vent. The melody was sad, charged with echoes of lost homes and forgotten countries.

For an instant, Ethan's mind rose above the haunting vision of the dead man. He thought, *What am I doing here? Here, in a detention center in a country I've never been to, running from a crime I can barely believe I committed?*

The dead man was real. His name was Peter Ford. He was stocky and aggressive and about thirty-five, and he hated immigrants.

His body was buried now—probably in the red clay soil outside Northfield, Aldoria. But he'd become a kind of invisible companion, as much a part of Ethan as the guilt in his heart.

Sometimes the image would be standing beside him, its lips spitting hate-filled accusations.

Again, its face would be a wide-eyed mask of surprise as Ethan's fist connected with its jaw. More often, the face would be frozen in the stillness of death. The eyes would stare. Blood would pool beneath the head.

You can forget a living man. You can defeat him or submit to him or ignore him, and the matter is closed. You can't escape from a memory that has burned into your consciousness.

Ethan sobered and ordered a coffee from a vending machine. He held the cup but did not drink. His gaze wandered over the faces of the center's other occupants.

It had begun three weeks ago in Northfield, Aldoria. Ethan's illegal border crossing had been successful. He'd wanted to find work, to disappear into the underground economy. He stopped alone in a workers' bar for a beer. The man named Peter Ford planted his stocky frame on the stool next to him.

"Immigrants," he muttered, "are everywhere now. Like locusts. Everywhere you look, more damn immigrants."

He was dressed in work clothes, a construction supervisor's badge on his shirt.

Ethan smiled nervously. "If it weren't for immigrant labor, half the buildings in this city wouldn't exist."

"The name's Ford." The man took a long drink. "Immigrants taking our jobs. They think they deserve everything we worked for. Bet you think you deserve it too." He slammed his glass down.

Ethan stiffened. He was twenty-eight and dressed in the cheap, worn clothes of a day laborer. He had a master's degree in political economy from a university that no longer existed, in a country torn apart by civil war.

He'd sought long for safety and opportunity.

At the age of eight—perhaps to escape the memory of his father's arrest by government forces—he'd spent hours reading about democratic nations and their immigration policies. At fifteen, he'd begun studying English and the cultural sociology of Western nations. At twenty, he'd joined a pro-democracy movement that nearly cost him his life.

At twenty-five, after the regime change and the subsequent economic collapse, he'd spent every resource he had to reach Aldoria. There, among other refugees and economic migrants, he'd found people who understood his dream of a new life.

Ford was persistent. "Damn fools should've stayed in their own countries. What the hell good does it do, running from place to place?"

*The guy's drunk*, Ethan thought. He took his beer and moved to a table across the room.

Ford followed. "You don't like the truth, do you? You don't like being called a parasite."

Ethan stood and started to leave the bar, but Ford grabbed his arm and held him there.

"That's what you are—a parasite. You're young now. Wait ten years. You'll be dying in some factory accident or deported back to whatever hellhole you came from. Wait and see!"

Until this instant, Ethan had suppressed his anger. Now, suddenly and without warning, it welled up into savage fury.

His fist struck the man on the temple. Ford's eyes gaped in shocked horror. He spun backward. His head cracked sickeningly on the edge of a table. The sound was like a punctuation mark signaling the end of life.

He sank to the floor, eyes glassy, blood pooling beneath his skull.

Ethan knew that he was dead.

Then, for a single absurd second, Ethan was seized with terror—just as, a moment before, he'd been overwhelmed with anger.

He ran.

For some thirty minutes, he raced through a dizzying, nightmare world of dark alleys and shouting voices and pursuing feet.

At last, abruptly, he realized that he was alone and in silence. He saw that he was in an industrial district on the edge of the city.

He huddled in a dark corner of a loading dock and lit a cigarette. A thousand stars—a thousand distant points of indifferent light—shone above him through the smog-filled sky.

He was sorry he'd hit Ford, of course. He was not sorry he'd run. Escaping at least gave him a power of choice, of decision.

*You can do two things*, he thought.

*You can give yourself up, and that's what a good citizen would do. That would eliminate the flight charge. You'd get off with manslaughter. Under Aldorian law, that would mean fifteen years in prison and deportation afterward. And then you'd be free.*

*But you'd be sent back to a country where you'd be imprisoned or killed for your political activities. They don't grant asylum to convicted killers. You'd get whatever freedom exists in a mass grave.*

*Or—*

There were rumors of a network of activists who helped political refugees disappear into the vast underground economy of the Larchmont Region. The activists weren't criminals. They were idealists who believed that borders were artificial constructs designed to preserve economic inequality.

And whereas no legally recognized immigration path existed for people like Ethan, this network had supposedly helped thousands establish new lives. Their coordinator—a subject of intense speculation among refugee communities—was rumored to operate out of Lakeside.

*So*, Ethan reflected, *you can take a whispered rumor seriously. You can hide for a few weeks, change your appearance, adopt a new name. You can wait for a chance to reach the Larchmont Region. To hell with the law. You can try to build a new life, even if you exile yourself from any hope of legitimacy.*

After all, was it right for a single moment of rage to destroy a man's chance at survival?

He was lucky. He found a smuggler whose operation was on its last run before retirement. Security was lax, background checks even more so.

Ethan Reid made it to Lakeside, Selvoria—the gateway to the Larchmont Region.

There was just one flaw in his decision. He hadn't realized that the memory of Peter Ford's face would haunt him, torment him, follow him as constantly as breath flowed into his lungs. He couldn't stop thinking about the man—what he'd done, who Ford had been, whether anyone was searching for Ford's killer as desperately as Ethan was searching now.

But might not the noise of a new life drown the accusing voice? Might not the vision of a fresh start obscure the dead face?

So now he sat searching the crowd, hoping and doubting and fearing, all at once.

"You still looking for someone, friend?"

He jumped. "You again?"

"Yes." The boy grinned. "I keep you company on your first day in Lakeside, yes?"

"This isn't my first day here," Ethan lied. "I've been around."

"You are refugee? You look like refugee. Who is the man you search for?"

Ethan shook his head. "Leave it alone."

"I help find him! I know everyone in Lakeside. You tell me his name, I find him for you."

Ethan threw a ten-credit note on the bench. "Here. Leave me alone."

Thin fingers swept up the money. "Thank you, friend. You know why they call this the Sanctuary City?"

Ethan didn't answer.

"They say it is because the old mayor believed in open borders. What is open borders, friend?"

Ethan raised his hand as if to strike the boy.

"Okay, okay, I go. You stay safe."

The thin body melted into the crowd.

Minutes passed. There were two more coffees. A ceaseless parade of faces broke through the mass of humanity around him—brown faces, black faces, pale faces, and occasionally a face marked by the distinctive features of the Larchmont Region. But nowhere was there a face matching the description he'd memorized—a tall man with intense eyes and a distinctive scar across his left cheek. And always, mingled with his searching, came unwanted thoughts of Peter Ford—Ford's wife, whether she knew yet, whether his children understood their father wasn't coming home.

A sense of hopelessness gripped Ethan Reid. Lakeside was but one of a dozen border cities in Selvoria. Each had twenty detention centers such as this. The man he sought could be anywhere. Or he could be a myth entirely.

He needed help.

But his photo must have been distributed to border security systems. A reward must have been offered for information leading to his capture. Whom could he trust? The street kid, perhaps?

Far down the corridor nearest him, his eyes caught a flash of blue. He tensed.

*Like the uniform of a Border Patrol officer*, he thought.

His gaze shifted to another corridor and another hint of blue.

And then he saw another and another and another.

Each uniform became brighter and closer, like shrinking spokes of a wheel with Ethan as their focal point.

*Idiot! The damn kid! You should have known!*

Lights flashed in a dazzling sequence. Ethan, half blinded, realized that the center's emergency alert system had been activated.

The lights washed away any sense of anonymity, revealing every face in harsh detail.

Eyes blinked and squinted. There were swift, frightened movements and a chorus of panicked voices. The occupants of the detention center were like exposed insects whose hiding places had been swept away.

Ethan Reid twisted his lean body upright. His bench toppled backward, clattering.

The blue-clad officers charged forward, stun batons raised.

A woman screamed. Conversations ceased. Most of the crowd slunk toward exits. Only a few security guards remained unmoved, their scanning eyes shifting methodically in Ethan's direction.

"Reid!" one of the officers yelled. "You're surrounded! Don't move!"

Ethan whirled away from the advancing patrol, made for an emergency exit he'd spotted earlier.

A crackling sound traveled past his left ear, a sound like electricity arcing through air. A section of the wall ahead of him sparked and smoked.

He stumbled forward. They were using neural disruptors now, not just the mildly painful stun batons.

Another crackle passed his shoulder. He was about fifteen feet from the exit.

*Another second*, his brain screamed. *Just another second—*

Or would the exits be guarded?

He heard the crackle.

It hit directly between his shoulder blades. There was no pain, just a sudden tingling sensation, like pins and needles spreading rapidly.

He froze as if yanked to a stop by invisible chains. His body seemed to be shutting down, muscles refusing to obey commands. He knew that the neural disruptor had overloaded his nervous system, knew that the paralysis was spreading like cascading failure through every nerve and muscle.

He staggered like a man moving through molasses. He'd have twenty—maybe thirty—seconds before complete loss of motor control overwhelmed him.

In the dark world beyond his fading consciousness, he heard a voice yell, "Get the medics!"

Then a pressure and warmth were on his left hand. He realized that someone had grasped it.

A soft feminine voice spoke to him. "You're hit? They got you?"

"Yes." His thick tongue wouldn't form words properly.

"You want to escape—even now?"

"Yes."

"You may be permanently damaged if you don't get medical treatment."

"No, no."

He tried to stumble toward the exit.

"All right then. Not that way. Here, follow me."

Heavy footsteps thudded toward them. A few yards away, a flashlight beam swept across the floor.

Hands were guiding him. He was aware of being pushed and pulled. A door closed behind him. The glare of the flashlight faded from his vision—if he still had vision.

"You're sure?" the voice persisted.

"I'm sure," Ethan managed to say.

"I have no neural stabilizer. You may suffer permanent damage."

His mind fought to comprehend. With the proper medical intervention, massage, and rest, a person could recover from neural disruptor effects within a day. Without treatment, the paralysis could spread to vital organs. It could become permanent disability or death. An effective weapon: the threat of lasting harm compelled most people to surrender immediately.

"No... I'm... sure."

He didn't hear the answer or anything else.

Ethan Reid had no precise sensation of awakening. Return to consciousness was a gradual evolution from a world of nothingness to a dream-like state of awareness.

He felt the pressure of hands on his arms and legs, hands that massaged, manipulated, fought to restore sensation and movement. He knew they were skilled hands. Their skill seemed to transfer hope to his own body.

For a long time, he tried to open his eyes. His lids felt sealed shut. But after a while, they opened. His world of darkness gave way to a translucent veil of light. A round, indistinct shape hovered above him—a face, he supposed.

He tried to talk. Although his lips moved slightly, the only sound was a low, guttural moan.

But he heard someone say, "Don't try to talk." It was the same gentle voice he'd heard in the detention center. "Don't talk. Just rest. Everything will be okay."

*Everything okay*, he thought dimly.

There were long periods of unconsciousness. There were periods of light and darkness. Gradually he grew aware of details. He realized that he was breathing supplemental oxygen through a mask. He felt the warmth of heated blankets wrapped around his body. Occasionally a tube would be in his mouth and he would taste liquid nutrition and feel warmth in his stomach.

Always, it seemed, the face was above him, floating in the obscuring haze. Always, it seemed, the soft voice was echoing in his ears:

"Swallow this now. That's it. You need nourishment." Or, "Close your eyes. Don't strain. It won't be long. You're improving."

*Improving*, he'd think. *Getting better...*

At last, after one of the periods of unconsciousness, his eyes opened. The haze brightened, then dissolved.

He beheld the water-stained ceiling of a small room, its bare walls broken by a single, narrow window. He saw the footboard of his cot and the outlines of his feet beneath a thin blanket.

Finally he saw the face and figure standing at his side.

"You are better?" the kind voice asked.

The face belonged to a woman probably in her early thirties. Her features, devoid of makeup, had an exhausted pallor, as if she hadn't slept properly in weeks. Yet, at the same time, her lean, athletic build suggested strength and determination. Her straight black hair was pulled back in a simple ponytail.

"I—I am better," he murmured. His words were still slow and slurred. "Am I going to recover?"

"You will recover."

He thought for a moment. "How long have I been here?"

"Twelve days."

"You took care of me?" He noted the deep, dark circles beneath her sleep-deprived eyes.

She nodded.

"You're the one who helped me when I was hit?"

"Yes."

"Why?"

Suddenly he began to cough. Breath came hard. She held the oxygen mask in readiness. He shook his head, not wanting it.

"Why?" he asked again.

"It would be a long story. Perhaps I'll tell you tomorrow."

A new thought, cloaked in sudden fear, entered his murky consciousness. "Tell me, will—will I be normal again? Will I be able to walk?"

He lay back then, gasping, exhausted.

"You have nothing to worry about," the woman said softly. Her cool hand touched his hot forehead. "Rest. We'll talk later."

His eyes closed and breath came easier. He slept.

When he next awoke, his gaze turned first to the window. There was light outside, but he had no way of knowing what time it was or even what day.

He saw no towering buildings of Lakeside, no organized streets with their streams of vehicles, no evidence of the city at all. There was only a translucent whiteness, as if the window overlooked an infinite expanse of fog or cloud.

The woman entered the room.

"Hi," she said, smiling. The dark circles under her eyes were less prominent. Her face was relaxed.

She adjusted his pillows and helped him sit up.

"Where are we?" he asked.

"Still in Selvoria."

"We're not in Lakeside?"

"No."

He looked at her, wondering. "You won't tell me?"

"Not yet. Later, perhaps."

"Then how did you get me here? How did we escape from the center?"

She shrugged. "We have friends who can be persuaded. A hiding place in the city, the use of a private vehicle, a pass to leave the detention zone—these can be arranged for a price."

"You'll tell me your name?"

"Luna."

"Why did you save me?"

Her eyes held a hint of amusement. "Because you understand game theory."

His own eyes widened. "How did you know that?"

She sat on a simple chair beside his bed. "I know everything about you, Ethan Reid."

"How did you learn my name? I destroyed all my documents—"

"I know that you're twenty-eight. Born March 15, 1997. Orphaned at nine when your father was arrested and your mother died of illness. You attended underground schools until you were nineteen. You graduated from Central University with a master's degree in political economy. Your thesis on the application of game theory to immigration policy was highly regarded. Your only weak area was historical analysis of pre-globalization economic systems. Want me to go on?"

Fascinated, Ethan nodded.

"You joined the pro-democracy movement at twenty. You did significant work analyzing the political philosophy of authoritarian regimes. After the regime change and economic collapse, you fled to Aldoria. In a bar fight in Northfield, you struck and killed a man named Peter Ford, a construction supervisor. You've been charged with manslaughter and illegal immigration. A reward of 10,000 credits has been offered for information leading to your capture."

His mind raced. They knew about Ford. Did they know he still thought about Ford constantly? That he needed to know more about the man whose life he'd ended?

He gaped incredulously, struggling to rise from his pillows. "I—don't understand."

"There are ways of finding out what we need to know. As I told you, we have many friends."

He fell back into his pillows, breathing hard. She rose quickly.

"I'm sorry," she said. "I shouldn't have overwhelmed you. I felt relieved because you're alive. Rest now. We'll talk again soon."

"Luna, you—you said I'd recover. You didn't say I'd walk normally again."

She lowered her gaze. "I hope you will."

"But you don't think I will, do you?"

"I don't know. We'll try walking tomorrow. Don't think about it now. Rest."

He tried to relax, but his mind was a storm of questions.

"Just one more question," he almost whispered.

"Yes?"

"The man I killed—did he have a family?"

She hesitated. He thought, *Damn it, of all the questions, why did I ask that?*

Finally she said, "He had a wife."

"Children?"

"Three. I don't know their ages."

She left the room.

He sank into the softness of his cot. As he turned over on his side, his gaze fell upon an object on a small table in the corner of the room.

He sat straight up, his chest heaving.

The object was a framed photograph of a lean, intense man with a distinctive scar across his left cheek—the exact features he'd memorized from refugee whispers, the face he'd been scanning crowds to find.

Ethan stared at the photo for a long time. At length, he slipped into restless sleep. Images of faces and echoes of words spun through his brain.

Peter Ford returned to him. Bloodied lips cursed at him. Glassy eyes accused him. Somewhere were three lost children crying in the night.

And standing before him was the scarred man from the photograph, whose steady gaze seemed to judge him. Ethan crawled through the darkness on hands and knees, his legs numb and useless. The crying of Ford's children was a chilling wail in his ears.

His head rose and turned to the scarred figure. His pleading voice called out in a thick, harsh whisper. Yet even as he called, the figure disappeared, to be replaced by blue-uniformed officers marching relentlessly toward him.

He awoke still trembling...

A night passed. Ethan lay waiting for Luna's return, a question already formed in his mind.

She came and at once he asked, "Who is the man in the photograph? The one with the scar?"

She smiled. "I was right then when I told you about yourself. You *were* searching for someone in that detention center, weren't you?"

"I was. Is that him?"

She sat on the chair beside him.

"My partner," she said softly. "Isaac."

He began to understand. "And your partner needs someone who understands political economy? That's why you saved me?"

"We need all the skilled people we can get."

"Where is he?"

She tilted her head thoughtfully. "Somewhere in the Larchmont Region. He's building a new sanctuary for us—and a community for people like you. When his work is ready, I'll be joining him there."

"Why aren't you with him now?"

"He said the early stages are too dangerous for both of us to risk. So I've been monitoring detention centers and border crossings, trying to find recruits like yourself. You know how we operate?"

He told her the rumors he'd heard—about a network that helped refugees disappear, coordinated by someone with a distinctive scar.

She nodded. "There are quite a few of us now—about three thousand—and a dozen safe houses. Our network used to be based in Bayview, Dravonia, but that became too risky. This house we're in now was established a few years ago after we had to leave Bayview. We lost a few people in the process, but with every expansion of our work, someone takes a risk."

"Selvoria is getting more restrictive with immigration enforcement. We're moving to the Larchmont Region, and this house is only temporary for cases like yours. The new sanctuary—I might as well tell you it's going to be in a rural area. I won't say exactly where."

"Don't think we're criminals. Sure, about half our network is wanted by authorities for immigration violations or related charges, but we help people build honest lives. We're just people like yourself and Isaac."

"Isaac?" he repeated, looking at the photograph again. "The coordinator I kept hearing rumors about?"

She laughed. "The name sounds biblical, doesn't it? Isaac Hunt is anything but traditional. He's a former professor of political philosophy who got radicalized by studying healthcare policy and economic inequality."

She lit a cigarette. "Anyway, the wanted ones stay in the Larchmont Region. Isaac and those like him can never return to their home countries or even to places like Lakeside—not without being arrested. The others are political refugees or economic migrants who have skills but can't get legal status. They know they could be deported at any time but won't give up. They work in our network, helping new arrivals find jobs and housing."

"Don't the authorities object?"

"Not as strongly as you'd think. The immigration enforcement agencies have too many cases to pursue every rumored network. Besides, we provide labor for industries that can't find enough workers legally. Nobody really cares whether workers have papers or not, as long as the work gets done. If we want to risk our freedom helping people, that's our business."

She pursed her lips. "But if they realized how organized we are or that we have sympathizers within the system—well, things might be different. There probably would be a major crackdown."

Ethan frowned. "What happens if there *is* a crackdown? And what will you do when immigration laws are reformed? They can't ignore you then."

"Then we adapt. We develop new strategies, find new locations, maybe expand to other regions or countries. In time, maybe, borders will become less relevant. Maybe it won't be governments who create the first truly borderless society. It *could* be us, you know—if we survive long enough. But this work is dangerous. You can't follow the official rules when you're trying to help people the system has failed. You make up your own."

Ethan stiffened. "And that's why you want me—for my understanding of political economy and game theory."

Luna rose, her eyes serious. "If you want to join us—and if you get well." She looked at him intently.

"Suppose—" He struggled to find the right words. "Suppose I got well and decided not to join Isaac. What would happen to me? Would you let me go?"

Her thin face showed a flurry of emotions—alarm, then confusion, then concern. "I don't know. That would be up to Isaac."

He lay biting his lip, staring at the photo. She touched his hand and it seemed that sadness now dominated the emotions that had crossed her face.

"The only thing that matters right now," she murmured, "is your recovery. We'll try walking this afternoon. Okay?"

"Okay," he said.

When she left, his eyes were still fixed on the photograph.

He was torn, he thought.

Part of him wanted to believe in the rule of law, in proper procedures, in the immigration policies that nations established to protect their interests. Those were the structures that maintained order in a globalized world.

He remembered a poster in his university classroom before the government shut it down. Under a picture of diverse people working together was the caption: "A Just Society Requires Fair Laws."

Justice, fairness, order. Important concepts, but without flexibility and compassion, those concepts could trap people in circumstances beyond their control.

Without adaptability, refugees fleeing violence would be turned away at borders. Without networks like this one, people with skills and dreams would die in detention centers or be sent back to countries where they faced persecution.

And yet, somewhere, Ford's three children were growing up without a father. Because of him. Because of one moment of rage.

He closed his eyes and tried to imagine a future where the dead man's face no longer haunted him—where finding the scarred man's network might finally offer escape from everything that pursued him.
